# SideNav

A vertical navigation rail, grouped into named sections.

```tsx
import { SideNav } from "@rata/react";
```

| | |
|---|---|
| Registry name | `side-nav` |
| Family | navigation |
| Tier | free |
| Status (css / react / figma) | latest / latest / future |
| Depends on | `state-layer`, `icon` |

## Behavior

A `<nav>` containing one list per section. No primitive and no keyboard handling: every link is its own tab stop, which is what navigation should be. Unlike TopNav this claims no page-level landmark beyond the nav itself — where the rail sits, and whether it is inside a `<main>` or beside it, is the caller's layout decision.

- **Sections are the only shape, even for a flat list** — A side nav exists because there are enough destinations to group; a flat one is the special case, not the default. Offering both `items` and `sections` would mean two mutually exclusive props and a rule about which wins — so a flat nav is one unlabelled section, which costs a pair of braces and removes the ambiguity entirely.
- **A section's label names its list rather than being a heading** — Same reasoning as Notice's title: a nav cannot know what heading level it sits under, and a wrong one breaks heading navigation for the whole page. The label is a plain element with an id, and the list points at it with `aria-labelledby` — so the group is announced with its name and the document outline is untouched.
- **Collapsing to an icon-only rail is out of scope** — A collapsed rail hides the labels, which is the point of collapsing and also the problem: a sighted reader then needs the name on hover, and this system has no Tooltip. Shipping the collapse without one would trade an accessible nav for a row of unexplained glyphs. It belongs with a Tooltip, not before one.
- **The current page is stated per item, as in TopNav** — Only the caller knows whether /invoices/123 counts as being on /invoices. Matching a path here would have to guess between exact and prefix and would be silently wrong for someone either way.

## Props

Extends `Omit<HTMLAttributes<HTMLElement>, "children">`.

| Prop | Type | Default | Summary |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sections` | `SideNavSection[]` | — | The destinations, grouped. One unlabelled section is a flat nav. |
| `label?` | `string` | `"Sections"` | Accessible name for the navigation landmark. |
| `className?` | `string` | — | Extra classes on the nav, for placement — not for restyling it. |

### `sections`

```ts
sections: SideNavSection[]
```

The destinations, grouped. One unlabelled section is a flat nav.

**Use when**

- A named section per group of related pages: "Billing", "Settings".
- A single section with no `label` when there is nothing to group.

**Don't use for**

- A section per item. A group of one is a heading over nothing, and it reads as a mistake.
- Actions. Everything here is announced as a destination and rendered as a link.

**Accessibility** Each section is a list; a labelled one is pointed at its own label with `aria-labelledby`, so the group is announced with its name. The count and order within each come free with the list.

### `label`

```ts
label?: string = "Sections"
```

Accessible name for the navigation landmark.

**Use when**

- Naming it for what it contains — "Invoices" for the rail inside that area — so it is distinguishable from the top nav in a landmark list.

**Don't use for**

- Leaving the default when a page also has a `TopNav`. Two navigation landmarks need distinct names, and that is the one place they matter most.
- The word "navigation", which the role already says.

**Accessibility** Becomes the `<nav>`'s `aria-label`.

### `className`

```ts
className?: string
```

Extra classes on the nav, for placement — not for restyling it.

**Use when**

- Giving the rail its width, or making it stick — both layout decisions the component deliberately leaves to the page.

**Don't use for**

- Changing the item treatment. The current-page marker is load-bearing, and a rail that marks it differently from the top nav reads as a different product.

## Use cases

### A grouped rail inside one area of the product

The commonest case: enough pages that they need grouping.

```tsx
<SideNav
  label="Invoices"
  sections={[
    {
      label: "Billing",
      items: [
        { label: "Invoices", href: "/invoices", current: true },
        { label: "Credit notes", href: "/credit-notes" },
      ],
    },
    {
      label: "Setup",
      items: [
        { label: "Tax rates", href: "/tax" },
        { label: "Templates", href: "/templates" },
      ],
    },
  ]}
/>
```

`label` names the landmark for what the rail contains, not for where it sits — "Invoices", not "Side". A page with a `TopNav` as well has two navigation landmarks, and that is exactly when the names earn their keep.

### A flat rail, with nothing to group

Few enough destinations that a heading over them would be noise.

```tsx
<SideNav
  label="Settings"
  sections={[
    {
      items: [
        { label: "Profile", href: "/profile", current: true },
        { label: "Notifications", href: "/notifications" },
        { label: "Security", href: "/security" },
      ],
    },
  ]}
/>
```

One section with no `label`. The braces are the cost of there being a single shape rather than two props that cannot both be used — the contract's reasoning for that is in the behaviour notes.

### Don't: a section for every item

Never — this is the shape to recognise and avoid.

```tsx
{/* Don't: three headings over one link each. */}
<SideNav
  sections={[
    { label: "Invoices", items: [{ label: "All invoices", href: "/invoices" }] },
    { label: "Clients", items: [{ label: "All clients", href: "/clients" }] },
  ]}
/>
```

Don't. A group of one is a heading over nothing: it doubles the reading length, and a screen reader announces a list of one item under a name that repeats it. Those are two flat items in one unlabelled section.

## Real usage in this repo

```tsx
<SideNav
        className="pg-rail"
        label="Settings"
        sections={[
          {
            items: [
              { label: "Profile", href: "#", current: true },
              { label: "Notifications", href: "#" },
              { label: "Security", href: "#" },
            ],
          },
        ]}
      />
```

## Token recipe

### base

The rail. No background of its own: it sits on whatever surface the page gives it, so the same component works against the canvas and inside a panel. Its width is the page's to set.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| padding-block | `space.padding.sm` |
| padding-inline | `space.padding.sm` |
| gap between sections | `space.stack.md` |

### section

A named group. The label is the list's accessible name, not a heading — a nav cannot know what heading level it sits under.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| label colour | `theme.fg.muted` |
| label font-size | `type.supporting.size` |
| label font-weight | `type.label.weight` |
| label text-transform | `type.label.text-transform` |
| gap between label and items | `space.stack.2xs` |
| gap between items | `space.stack.2xs` |

### item

One destination, filling the rail's width so the whole row is the target.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| colour | `theme.fg.secondary` |
| font-size | `type.control.size.sm` |
| font-weight | `type.control.weight` |
| block-size | `size.control.md` |
| padding-inline | `space.control.padding-inline.sm` |
| border-radius | `radius.element` |
| gap between icon and label | `space.gap.sm` |
| icon size | `size.icon.text` |
| hover / press | `compose the .rata-state-layer class` |
| focus ring | `theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible` |

### item-current

The page you are on. A tinted row plus an edge marker, alongside aria-current, so the state is never carried by colour alone.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| background | `theme.accent-role.subtle` |
| colour | `theme.fg.primary` |
| indicator | `theme.accent-role.bg at border.2, space.4 tall and centred on the inline-start edge` |
